chapters.title: The Things She Could Not Replace
paragraphs: The first of July arrived wearing a thin, unconvincing sunlight, the kind the monsoon allows for an hour to make you careless about umbrellas. Zero woke before the alarm with the sensation of having been told something in his sleep. The crane was on the desk, beak toward the window, exactly where it had been left. The journal was open. Beneath Held. and Noticed., in pink, a third line had appeared in the night, and when he leaned close to read it the ink was still faintly damp: Today she will lose something small. He did not know whether it was a warning or a diagnosis. He closed the book, which he had never done before without finishing the page, and went to work.

He saw her before she saw him, which was a rare advantage, and he spent it badly, by simply standing in the corridor outside the Analytics room with his bag against his chest. She was wearing royal blue. It was a shirt with thin pale-blue stripes running down it like the lines of a ruled page, tucked into khaki trousers, and the combination should have been severe and was instead the opposite: a girl dressed for an exam she had already decided to ace. Her hair was tied back loosely. At her collar sat a small brooch he had not seen before, a bowtie, no bigger than a thumbnail, studded with tiny diamanté stones that threw the corridor light across the ceiling in a scatter of sparks. She had the walk of someone who has dressed carefully and is pretending she has not. He thought of a thing he had said on the sixteenth of June, half joking, in the first hour of knowing her, when he had asked whether she was a goddess and added, because the migraine had made him honest, that he had never realised prayers could be this potent. She had laughed at him then. He thought now that it had not been a joke at all, only the first accurate sentence he had ever said aloud.

And then, as he watched, the bowtie gave way. There was no drama in it. The tiny clasp simply let go, and the brooch dropped from her collar, and she caught it against her chest with the quick reflex of a cricketer, and looked down at it in her palm. One of the wings had come away from the centre. The stones glittered, perfectly intact, and the thing itself was ruined. She turned it over once, twice, with her thumb. "Oh," she said, to no one, in a voice so small that he almost did not hear it, and he had the odd sense that the corridor had gone quieter around the word.

By the time he reached her desk she had pinned her face back into order, but the order was a little off, like a picture hung a degree crooked. "It's fine," she said. "It's just a bow." She set the pieces in a small zipped pouch and put the pouch in her bag. Then, with her hand still in the bag, she went very still, and he watched the stillness travel up her arm and into her face, and she said, in the same small voice, "My earbuds."
"What about them?"

"They're not here." She went through the bag, the way people do when they know already, with the thoroughness of ritual: the front pocket, the side pocket, the inner zip, the pouch with the pen, the pouch with the cards. She turned out a lipstick, a hair tie, a roll of tissues, a pack of mints, a folded form. She turned out the bag itself and shook it gently, as one shakes a sleeping thing, to be sure. "They were in my hand yesterday. I was on the bus. I had them on the bus." She said it three times, each time more quietly, as if the repetition might rewind something. "I don't understand. They were right here."

Zero said the worst possible thing in the worst possible voice, which was a calm, helpful one. "It's okay," he said. "We'll get you a new pair. I'll order them right now. Same model, there's a sale on, you'll have them by Friday." He had the phone out. He was already scrolling, his thumb moving with the brisk competence of a man fixing a bug. "You've used these a lot, right? So you've got your value out of them. That's the whole point of a gift, it does what it's for, and then it's—" He stopped, because she had looked up.

It was not an angry look. That would have been easier. It was the look of someone who has held out something warm and watched it being weighed. "No," she said, quietly. "They weren't that kind of thing." And then she turned her chair a few degrees toward her screen and began, with great concentration, to open a spreadsheet she did not need. He sat with the phone in his hand and the shopping page glowing on it, a list of identical white earbuds in a grid, each one with a price and a rating and a small cheerful picture, and he understood with a cold, clear click that he had made a category error so large that it had a floor plan. You never asked me to be more than I was, but you made me want to become more. He would write that sentence one day, in a pink he could not yet account for, and it would be true because of mornings like this one, when she asked him for nothing at all and he saw, too late, exactly what he had failed to be. He had tried to solve her. She had not wanted to be solved. She had wanted him to sit beside the loss and let it be as large as it was, and he had priced it instead.

He tried to repair it, which was the second mistake. For an hour he was a model of silent competence, bringing her water, bringing her a printout she had not asked for, fixing a formatting error in a cell she had not noticed. She thanked him for each of them in the flat polite voice one uses for waiters, and every thank-you was a small door closing in a corridor he could not see the end of. At eleven he went and stood by the window with his forehead against the cool glass and thought, with the old, ugly clarity of a man who has been through this before in other buildings, I should have let her vent. That was all. She had not needed a plan. She had needed a witness. And a witness, he thought, was the thing he was supposed to be good at.

He went back to her desk. He did not touch her. He did not say I'm sorry, which would have been a request for absolution, or I'll find them, which would have been another plan. He pulled the empty chair from the next desk and sat down beside her, a little too close, with his shoulder an inch from hers, and said, "Tell me about them."
Her hands stopped on the keys.
"I don't mean to fix it," he said. "I'm not going to fix it. I just want to know what they were."

She did not say anything for a long moment. The air conditioning hummed. Somewhere behind them a printer woke and thought better of it. Then she said, in a voice that was not the waiter voice or the diva voice but a third one he had not heard, plain and a little hoarse: "They were a gift. From someone I love. I wasn't supposed to have them yet. It was an early one." She turned a pen over in her fingers. "I wore them through a whole hard year. Through exams, through my grandmother being ill, through an entire winter of not being able to sleep. They were the only thing that was mine while everything else was being decided. There's a song that's on them. It's not on my phone. It's only on them, because of how the person made the playlist. If I lose them I lose the song."
"You can't get the song back."

"I can get the song back. I can't get them back." She laughed, a small dry sound with nothing in it. "Do you know what's stupid? They were old. They hardly worked on the left side. I'd been meaning to replace them for months. And I couldn't, because replacing them would have meant admitting they were finished."

He nodded. He did not say anything. It was the hardest thing he had done that month, harder than the platform, harder than the cabinet: he sat with his own useless hands in his lap and let the thing be the size it was. He did not reach for a solution. He did not reach for her. He only breathed out, slowly, and let the silence become a place where she could put the whole of it down.
"It's not the earbuds," she said, after a while. "It's that it was mine, and it's gone, and nobody can tell me where."
"I know."
"You don't. But it's nice that you're sitting there."

He thought: I take photographs of everything because I cannot bear to lose anything. The thought arrived complete, like a letter pushed under a door. He had four thousand pictures of rooms and faces and the undersides of leaves, and each one was an earbud, each one a small, stubborn refusal to let a thing be lost without a witness. He had thought it was a flaw in his character, a form of greed. He had never once considered that it was the same thing she was doing, now, at her desk, with her face turned half away. It's the same disease, he thought, with a rush of tenderness so large that it frightened him. She keeps things because they carried her. I keep things because I'm afraid of the dark. It's one disease. We have the same disease.

On the far edge of his hearing, so faint that he could have dismissed it, a few bars of music began, thin and far away, as if played through a small speaker at the bottom of a well. He turned his head. Across the desk, she had stopped typing. Her head was tilted a little to the left, in the posture of someone listening to something in an ear that was not there.
"Do you hear that?" she said.
"Hear what?"

She frowned. The music cut off, as cleanly as a tap closing. "Nothing," she said. "I thought I—" And she touched her ear with two fingers, wonderingly, as one touches the place where a tooth used to be.

Object lost, said the clerical voice, in the soft, flat tone of a man closing a file. Object not erased. Reclassify: carrier of meaning. There was a pause, as though the voice were turning something over that it had not expected to find. Noted. The meaning stays when the object goes. And then, almost to itself, with the faint dismay of a bookkeeper who has found a column that does not balance: That is a problem.

At one, they went to lunch, and the party was smaller than it had been the day before. Her form-filling had swallowed the morning: she had a stack of paperwork for her college and a list on her phone, and between the one and the other she was buying gifts for her cousins, small things, bracelets and hair ties, a toy for the youngest, each chosen with the focused ferocity of a woman building a case. He did not ask whom they were for. He carried the shopping bag, and when she tried to take it back he shook his head, and she let it go with an eye-roll that was almost fond.

They waited at the canteen for the friend who was always last. A girl from the next desk bank, loud, loyal, famously late, arrived with a bag the size of a toddler and held it out to him with an enchanting look of expectation. "Hold this," she said. "You're a gentleman."
"No," said Zero.
"What?"
"I'm carrying one bag today. It's already assigned."

The girl stared at him. Then she looked at Ichi, who was studying the ceiling with an expression of such angelic innocence that it amounted to an alibi, and she put her hands on her hips and began to laugh, helplessly, a high delighted whoop that turned heads three tables away. "You refused me!"
"I'm a one-bag man."
"He's very loyal," said Ichi to the ceiling.
"He's a lunatic." But the girl took her own bag back, still laughing, and the whole table was in on it, the joke running down its length like a fuse.
The bill came at the end, and she reached for her purse and said, evenly, "We'll split."
"I'll pay."
"We split."
"You can pay after you start earning," said Zero. It sounded to him like a perfectly reasonable sentence. It sounded to the table like the opening line of a courtship.
"I am an intern. I earn a stipend," said Ichi. "I have a stipend."
"Then pay me back in that."
"With what? Respect?"

"With your stipend, in installments, with interest," said Zero, and for a moment she looked at him the way a chess master looks at an opponent who has just made a move that is either genius or blindness. Then she split the bill anyway, to the last coin, and slid his half across the table, and said, very low, so that only he could hear: "I will pay you back. Not in money. Don't make me say it."

Someone down the table was describing a planned event, a mock wedding for Friday, the kind of office theatre that happens when a floor needs a reason to laugh, with an invitation to be designed and a groom already nominated. "Gold font," said the organiser. "Cursive. Very royal."
"No," said Ichi, without looking up. "No gold font. If you do a gold font I will not attend."
"It's a wedding."
"It's a mock wedding. Gold font is for the real ones. We have standards." She turned to Zero with a face of perfect, grave neutrality and said, "Noted, my queen?"
"Noted," he said, though he had not been asked.
"I was talking to myself."
"I know. I noted it anyway."
Across the table, the loud girl, who had been waiting for a reason, raised her phone. "Wait. Hold on. Both of you. Don't move."
"No," said Ichi.
"One photo. For the team group."
"No pictures where I'm alone."

"You won't be alone. You're sitting right next to him. Come on. Look at the camera." And then, because the loud girl was a force of nature and not a diplomat: "Put something in your hair. Anything. Put a clip on him, it'll be funny."

It was a small black hair clip, the kind a girl keeps in her bag for emergencies and loses at the rate other people lose pens. She looked at it in her palm, and at Zero, and with the solemnity of a priestess performing a minor sacrament, she reached across the table and fastened it into his hair above the left ear. Her fingers were cool and quick. He felt the small pressure of the clip, the faint grazing of her knuckle against his temple. It lasted two seconds, and he would remember all of it.
"There," she said. "Now you're evidence."

She leaned in beside him, her shoulder against his, and the camera flashed, and when he looked at the screen afterwards, he saw himself: a tired man in a cherry-red shirt with a girl's clip in his hair, grinning like someone who had been handed a prize he did not know he had entered for. And beside him, in royal blue, laughing at something off the edge of the frame, she was not alone. She was in the picture. She was evidence of something, and she had chosen it. She will let me photograph her, he thought, as long as she isn't the only thing in the frame. It was a very small thought. It felt like a door opening in a wall he had been touching for weeks.

The afternoon was a corridor of small mercies. The Talker found them at three. He was the colleague everyone called by his initials, a man who could take any sentence you gave him and wring it dry, and he arrived at her desk with a stack of requirements and an expression of terrible friendliness, saying that he had a quick question about the reporting spec, a very quick one, which would take only a few minutes of her time. Zero watched her face change, slowly, like a sky. Forty minutes later the quick question had become a lecture on the history of the form, and she was nodding with the glassy, polite horror of a woman being talked at by a tide.

He did not decide to do it. He stood, and he picked up a folder, and he said in his most pleasant, most official voice, "Sorry to interrupt. I need her for the specification review. It's with the manager. It's urgent, and it's already late."
The Talker blinked. "But I haven't finished—"
"I know. We'll circle back." Zero smiled at him with a warmth that could have been used to melt chocolate. "Thank you so much for your patience."

She was beside him before the man could assemble a reply. They walked down the corridor side by side, fast, with the unhurried gait of people who have done nothing wrong, and when they reached the bend by the Analytics room, she stopped and pressed her back against the wall and began to laugh without a sound, her whole body shaking with it, one hand over her mouth.
"There's no review," she managed.
"No."
"There's no manager."
"There might be. I didn't check."
"You bailed me out." She wiped her eyes. "That's—I've been trying to leave for forty minutes. I was going to chew through my own arm."
"I noticed."

"You noticed." She was still laughing, but it had softened, and now there was a look in her face he had not seen before, an openness, like a window unlatched. "You noticed and you did something. You didn't ask. You didn't make a speech."
"I'm learning," said Zero.

She looked at him. The corridor was empty. Down at the far end, someone's phone rang and was answered. She was still leaning against the wall, with her bag hanging from her shoulder and her shoulders curling forward a little, the faint, tired slouch of someone who has been holding herself upright all day against a great deal of weather.

He opened his arms. He did not step toward her. He only held them open, a small width of air, an offer, an if you'd like. He thought: this has to be her decision, or it is not a hug. And he waited, and the corridor waited with him, and the long, slow second stretched until it had a grain.
She stepped in.

It was not graceful. It was the plain, hurried step of a person who has made up her mind, and then she was against him, her forehead below his chin and her hands between them, small and uncertain, and he put his arms around her and held on. She was so soft. He had not been prepared for that. He had thought of her all week as a kind of bright architecture, edges and decisions and quick light, and here was the other thing, the part she kept behind the architecture: warm and slight and breathing, her whole weight trusted to him in a single exhale. At first she held her shoulders high, a little rigid, still slouching into herself. He did not correct her. He waited, one hand spread between her shoulder blades, and slowly, by degrees, she let go, and straightened, and her spine unfolded against his palm like something remembering how.

He drew her head against his chest, gently, so that her ear lay over his heart. He felt her go still. He knew what she could hear. His pulse was running at an indecent speed, and he could do nothing about it, and he found that he did not want to. Let her hear it, he thought. Let her hear how much it is. She stayed there for a long time. Her breathing slowed against his shirt. At some point her hands came up and found the back of it, and gripped, lightly, as one holds onto a railing on a moving train.

The embrace softened into something he had no word for. It was warm and drowsy and entirely unhurried, and she had melted into it so completely that he thought, with a rush of tenderness, that she might fall asleep standing up. There was only the hum of the corridor and the smell of her hair, jasmine and rain, and the cool blue of her shirt against his arms. He held her, and he held her, and for the length of that minute he was not afraid of anything.

He had been about to kiss her cheek. He knew it as he knew his own name; his whole body had leaned toward it. But some quieter, wiser thing had caught him by the collar, and he thought, no, not that, not yet, not like a man helping himself. He turned his head and put his mouth to her forehead instead, softly, a long still pressure, the way you put a seal on something you mean to keep. She made a very small sound. When he drew back, her face was flushed to the hairline, her eyes were shut, and she was smiling, openly and helplessly, with the particular pink of a girl who has been caught being happy.
"You're blushing," he said.
"I'm warm," she said, with great dignity. "It's the air conditioning."
"It's very cold."
"Then it's the other thing." She opened her eyes. "Let me enjoy it."
So he did. He let her.

And in the stillness of that corridor, with her face against his collar and the whole slow afternoon on pause, he heard it again, faint and thin and from nowhere: a few bars of a song, played through a small speaker at the bottom of a well. This time it was not coming from the air. It was coming from the place where her ear was pressed to his chest. A tune she had carried through a hard year, rising from a place that was not a device, a place that had no battery and no left side that stopped working. And over it, steady as a metronome, the beat of his own heart, which she was listening to, and which was, he understood in a slow dazed wave, the first sound she would remember.

Heartbeat, said the clerical voice, very quietly. It did not sound pleased and it did not sound displeased. It sounded like a man standing at the edge of a field he had been told was empty. Candidate for retention. And a moment after, with something very close to alarm: Why does it not decay?

They went back toward the Analytics room together, a little apart now, with their faces arranged. At the door of the room, two colleagues were standing in the corridor, waiting for no one in particular, with the glazed, benevolent look of people who have been loitering on purpose. They were the same two women who had adopted Zero in his second week. They watched the two of them approach. One of them said, with an expression of perfect innocence, "Oh, hi. We were just standing here."
"For twenty minutes," said the other.
"It's very interesting standing."

Ichi looked at Zero. Zero looked at the ceiling. A beat passed, long enough for the whole corridor to hold its breath, and then the first colleague snorted, and the second one lost it entirely, and the sound went up and down the hall like a bell. Ichi began to laugh. Zero began to laugh. They went into the room laughing, all four of them, with the clean, hysterical relief of people who have been spared an explanation, and she dropped into her chair with her bag still on her shoulder, and he sat down across from her with the clip still in his hair.
"You forgot to take it out," she said.
"I'm keeping it."
"It's my last one."
"Then I'll guard it."

She shook her head. She was smiling so hard that it must have hurt. And on the edge of her desk, half hidden under a stack of forms, he saw the small zipped pouch with the broken bowtie in it, its stones glittering faintly through the plastic. He did not say anything. He thought, instead, of the lines in the pink ink, the third one, the one he had closed the book on: Today she will lose something small. It had been true. It had been exactly true, and it had not been the whole truth, and he thought now, with the humming certainty of a man who has begun to read a language: the thing she lost was never the thing she lost. He had been so afraid of losing and so careless about what a loss was made of. She had lost a pair of earbuds and a brooch. He had found, in the same hour, the sound of his own heartbeat in her ear.

At the window, the weak sunlight was beginning to fail. A rim of cloud had risen over the buildings across the road, the colour of an old bruise, and the first fat drops of the afternoon had started to strike the glass one at a time, as if someone were counting. She looked up at it. He saw her look, and he saw her think, and he knew, without being told, that there was a meeting that evening, the placement training, on her laptop, from six; that she had promised her friends she would log in for them; that it would be raining; and that he would not let her walk to the gate alone.

He did not know what would happen at the gate. He did not know what a taxi was, or a dashboard, or a minute. He knew only that on the corner of his desk, in the dying light, the paper crane had turned in the night to face the girl across the room, and that its left wing, the one with the thumbnail groove, was warm to the touch, as if someone had been holding it.
chapters.relic: the sentimental earbuds · Supporting: the diamond bowtie, the royal-blue outfit, the hair clip

chapters.title: The Hair Clip at 7:02
paragraphs: By six the rain had stopped pretending. It came down over the Analytics floor in long grey sheets that turned the windows into a smeared watercolour of the city, and the lights inside the office seemed to lean closer, as lights do when the weather outside has decided to be the more interesting thing. Zero had closed his laptop twice and opened it twice. He was waiting, with the self-conscious patience of a man who has told himself he is not waiting, for her to look up from her screen and announce that it was time. She had two windows open, a spreadsheet and a video call, and in the corner of the screen a small queue of names, her friends' names, each a separate login for a meeting she was attending on behalf of all of them at once.

"It's a placement session," she said, without turning. "Attendance is compulsory. If three of us aren't in it we all get a flag." She typed something, clicked something, and a second box blinked green. "So I'm three people tonight. Don't make that face."
"I'm not making a face."

"You have a face. It's the face you make when something is lovable and you've decided not to say so." She closed the lid of one laptop and opened the other, which was not hers, and Zero realised that she had borrowed a second machine from somewhere for exactly this. "There's a cab. I'm taking a cab. It's raining. And you are not walking me to the gate."
"I'm walking you to the gate."
"I said—"
"I heard you." He picked up the umbrella, the black one with the repaired spoke, and held it in front of him like a credential. "I'm walking you to the gate."

She looked at him for a long moment, and the corner of her mouth moved in that direction it had when it was losing an argument it had never intended to win. Then she swept the clip from the edge of her desk. It was the small black one, her last, the one he had worn all afternoon above his left ear, and which she had reclaimed at the lift with the brisk fingers of a woman recovering a hostage. She turned it over, once, in her palm, and held it with the phone in the same hand, the two small objects pressed together like a pair of stones.

The rain at the gate of the building was a different animal from the rain at the window. It had weight and direction and a voice. They stood under the narrow awning with the black umbrella between them and the whole street going silver at the edges, a river of tail lights, the hiss of tyres, a woman across the road clutching a plastic sheet over her head and laughing at the sky. The cab came out of the dark in a shiver of yellow and black, an old taxi with a cracked dashboard and a driver who looked as though he had been born inside it. She slid in first. She had her bag, and her borrowed laptop, and a small damp lunch box, and the umbrella that was hers, the bright confused one, which she shook once, closed, and passed to him through the door. "Hold that. Don't open it in here. Don't touch the floor. They're wet."
"I know how umbrellas work."
"You do not." And then, without looking at him, in the voice she used for small unguarded things: "Don't increase your walking speed. You always do. I can't keep up."
"I wasn't—"

"You were." She was settling into the corner of the seat with the laptop on her knees, opening it, sorting through a rattle of windows. "You do it when you're nervous. You walk faster. It's fine. Just stop."

He had not known that. He took it in, very carefully, the way one takes a small unexpected gift from a stranger, and noted that she had been watching his feet. He folded the black umbrella and set it beside the other on the floor, as instructed, with the handle out of the way, and he climbed in beside her and pulled the door shut against the rain. The cab smelled of wet vinyl and old incense and the cardamom of a thousand previous passengers' chai. The windscreen wipers went to work. The dashboard clock, a small green number glowing in the dark beneath the speedometer, said 6:51. He looked at it, and then, for no reason he could name, he looked at it again, and some animal part of his brain filed the number away as though it had been told that it would matter.
"The meeting's started," she whispered, as if the laptop might hear her. "I'm late for all three of us."
"Do you want me to hold it?"

She hesitated. It was the barest pause, a half-breath, and he understood that she was weighing a thing that had nothing to do with laptops. Then she slid the machine from her knees onto his, quite deliberately, and said, "Don't drop it. It isn't mine."

He balanced it. It sat across his thighs like a small hot animal, the screen tilted toward her, and she leaned over it from her side of the seat, close, with her shoulder against his arm and her face lit blue from below. She clicked and typed and muted and unmuted. There were three logins, he saw, three tiny rectangles with three names, and at the top of the screen a stern voice was already describing, in the cadence of a person reading from a slide, how to answer the question "tell me about yourself." He took one of his own earphones from his pocket, a small white thing, the wire tangled, and held it out to her without a word. She looked at it. She looked at the empty shape in her own ear where something else had lived for a year. She took it. She put it in her left ear, and he put the other in his right, and for a minute they were tied to each other by a few inches of wire and a stranger's voice describing the importance of eye contact.

Somewhere in the second minute, she leaned into him. It was not a decision. He felt the weight arrive, a small warm settling against his shoulder, the way a bird lands on a wire, and then her head was resting in the hollow below his collarbone as though it had always belonged there, and a loose strand of her hair was tickling his jaw. He did not look down. He held very still, with the laptop on his knees and the wire between them, and he thought: home stopped being a place. It was a sentence with no author and no past tense. Home stopped being a place the moment your hands made anywhere feel safe. He would write it one day, in a book that would not stay shut, but at that moment it was not a sentence at all. It was a cab on Lalbaug flyover in the rain, and a girl's head against his chest, and the whole shuddering interior of an old Premier Padmini transformed, by nothing more than her weight, into the most habitable room in the world.
"Come here," he had whispered, earlier, in the instant before she leaned, and he would never be certain afterwards whether he had said it aloud or only thought it so hard that she had heard.
She had come anyway. That was the truth of it. She had come without hesitation, as though the sentence had been written on a card she was already holding.

The cab slid through the evening like a boat on a canal. The streets of Parel were a flooded gold, shop signs bleeding into puddles, a man pushing a handcart through knee-high water, a bus with its windows steamed to blindness. The meeting droned on in his ear, and he could not have repeated a word of it. A voice described what an interviewer wants to see. Another said something about confidence. Beside him, the girl on his shoulder was fighting sleep with the dogged, doomed ferocity of a person who has been up since five and had one early lunch and a great many difficult conversations. Her typing slowed. Her eyelids fluttered between wakefulness and some other country. She sat up once, jerked, said "I'm listening, I'm listening," in a voice that had already left, and then she was sinking again, a little further each time.

He shifted her head, gently, with one hand. Her chin had dropped toward her chest at an angle that would have left her with a stiff neck by morning, and he put two fingers beneath it and lifted it, ever so carefully, until her head lay along his shoulder at the right slant. She murmured something. He did not catch the words. He put his cheek against the crown of her head and breathed in jasmine and rain and the faint cool scent of a girl who has been in air conditioning all day, and he felt the entire rest of his life narrow down to a few square inches of upholstery.

On her left wrist, the clover bracelet shivered with the movement of the cab. In her ears, a pair of small golden hoops caught the light of every passing streetlamp and threw it, in tiny arcs, across his sleeve. He had not noticed the hoops that morning. He noticed them now. They were thin, plain, rimmed with some faint scratch of wear, the sort of earrings one puts on every day for years until they become a part of the face. He watched the light slide along one of them. It was a small, ordinary, impossible thing, and it struck him that he would remember it for the rest of his life, and he took out his phone and then, with a flush of shame, put it back, because to photograph her now would have been to take something she had not offered.

Somewhere in the middle of the meeting, the phone and the clip slipped from her hand. He felt them go, a small clatter against the seat, the black clip and the phone with its cracked corner, sliding toward the gap between the cushions where small things go to be lost. He caught them before they fell, one in each hand, and looked at them for a moment as one looks at two small witnesses. She had been holding them, he realised, the whole way, against her chest, as one holds the things that matter. He thought about what the clip meant: her last, the one she had put in his hair, the only one she had left. He did not wake her. He opened her purse, which lay on the seat beside her, and set the phone inside, and the clip beside the phone, and closed the clasp with the slow care of a man closing a drawer in a sleeping house.
She stirred. "Mm."
"It's okay."
"I felt that." She did not open her eyes. Her voice was thick with sleep and entirely unembarrassed. "You took my stuff."
"I put it in your bag."
"I know." A pause, in which the wipers crossed the windscreen twice. "Thank you."

It was nothing. It was a sentence of two words, murmured into a stranger's shoulder, in a cab, in the rain, and Zero sat with it for a very long time. She had felt him do it. She had let him. She had trusted him to take two small objects out of her hands while she slept, which was a thing that nobody had ever trusted him with, and she had said thank you without opening her eyes, as one thanks a person one has no reason to doubt.

The voice in the earphone had reached a section about handling difficult questions. He did not hear it. He had a strange pressure behind his ribs, as though the word noticed were pressing against the inside of his chest and wanting out. She had noticed. She always noticed. And she had stayed silent, which was the better half of noticing, the half that said I know what you are doing and I am letting you do it.

The rain went on. The cab turned onto a long dark stretch of road lined with warehouses and banyan trees, and the light in the windows grew thin and amber. He held her. With his right arm he gathered her closer until she fit against him with a small sigh, her head tucked under his jaw and the whole length of her side pressed warm against his own, and he shifted his legs so that the laptop sat firm across his knees and could not slide. He kept his thighs tensed against it, braced against the door, because it was not his machine and it was not his to break, and because he had decided in some private cabinet of his mind that he would do this one thing perfectly if he did nothing else well all year. His hands, he found, were shaking slightly. They held her as though they had been designed for it: not tightly, not claiming, only supporting, the way a railing supports a person on a staircase.

She looked so small. That was the thing he could not get past. All week she had been a kind of weather, large and quick and impossible to stand against, and here she was in the corner of a seat with her laptop gone and her shoes slipped off at the heel and her mouth slightly open, impossibly small, impossibly precious, a person who had spent a long day holding up the sky and had finally been allowed to put it down. He began to talk to her. He did not decide to. A sound came out of him, low and wordless, the kind of cooing noise one makes to a sleeping child or a frightened bird, and he felt something in her ease. He pressed a kiss to her temple. Then another, a little to the left, in the soft hollow where the hair began. Each was a sentence he did not need to say aloud. I've got you. I'm here. Nothing is going to fall.

He stroked her arm, slowly, the length of it, from shoulder to wrist, in the way one calms a thing that is already calm. Every gentle pat rocked her further down into sleep. She would stir, and shift, and settle again a little closer, as if a tide were bringing her in. And then, without waking, she turned and wrapped both her hands around his arm, the one that held her, and hugged it to her chest like a small koala refusing to let go of a branch.
He forgot how to breathe.

It lasted a very long time, or a very short one. The meeting murmured in his ear. The wipers made their small rhythmic swish. He held absolutely still, afraid that if he moved an inch, if he so much as swallowed, the spell would break and the whole warm architecture of the evening would collapse into a taxi and a girl and a man with a laptop on his knees. He was too careful to adjust the screen, which had begun to tilt. He was too careful to shift the leg that was going numb. He had a sudden, vivid certainty that he would remember this stillness for the rest of his life, and that remembering it would be both the best and the worst thing that ever happened to him.

Retention, said the clerical voice, in the faintest whisper at the back of his skull. It did not sound clinical now. It sounded like someone leaning over a cradle. Contact held. Pulse matched. Duration: increasing. A pause. This is going to be difficult to remove.

Outside, a lorry went by in a gush of spray. The cab swayed. A streetlamp slid past, and the next, and the one after that, each laying a long amber stripe across her sleeping face, and he watched them come and go and thought, with the helpless wonder of a man who has been handed more than he can hold: I do not know what I did.

He did not know what came over him. Maybe it was the amber light on the windows. Maybe it was how peaceful she looked. Maybe it was only the overwhelming, uncomplicated realisation that he loved this girl far more than he had any words for, and that she was asleep against him with her hands around his arm, and that no one in the world knew. He leaned down. He kissed her cheek.

She let out the smallest sigh, the kind that escapes when someone is trying very hard to stay composed. It was not the sigh of a sleeper. He knew it at once, with the instinct of a man who has spent weeks learning the grammar of her breath. She was awake. She had been awake, perhaps, for a while. She was lying with her eyes closed and her hands on his arm, trying to be nonchalant about it, and failing, with a particular tenderness that nearly undid him.
He smiled. He could not help it. And against his shoulder, in the dark, he felt her smile too: a small curve, a shift of the cheek, a secret she was not quite keeping.

He kissed her cheek again. Slower this time. He let it linger, a heartbeat longer than a stolen thing should, because he wanted her to know it was not an accident. This is intentional, the kiss said. I am not afraid to do this, because I want to. He held it there until he felt her breath catch, and then he drew back an inch, and looked at her face in the amber dark.

Her eyes were open now. She was looking up at him from a distance of almost nothing, and there was nothing nonchalant left in her expression at all. Her forehead, he saw, was a little damp from the heat of the cab, and he realised that he had been kissing it all this time without noticing, in the intervals between everything else, that it had become familiar territory, a place where his affection had found its home. She did not look away. He did not look away. A silence passed between them that was a whole conversation, every word of it unspoken, and he thought: whatever happens next, I will not forget that she looked at me like this.
He lifted two fingers, very gently, and set them beneath her chin.

She did not resist. She let her face tilt up to him, an inch, then another, in the half-light, and her lashes lowered, and the earring at her ear threw a tiny scatter of gold across his wrist. The meeting went on murmuring in the earphone between them. Rain poured down the windows in long silver ropes. Somewhere ahead of them, the cab turned onto a bridge, and the city fell away on both sides into darkness and water, and the whole world seemed to hold its breath.
His eyes went, for no reason, to the dashboard.

The green numbers glowed in the dark. They had been 6:51 when he got in. Twenty minutes had passed, or an hour, or a thousand years. He read them the way one reads a word that one has been waiting to read all one's life.
That is where the chapter stops.

It stops there because the thing that happened next belongs to another page, in another chapter, in a voice that has not yet been permitted to tell it. There is a reason, and the reason is not cruelty. It is that some moments cannot be told at the speed they are lived. They have to be carried a long way first, through the whole dark middle of a story, and set down only when the reader is tall enough to bear their weight.

What can be said is this. At 7:02 the cab slowed, as though the road itself had paused. The wipers stopped mid-sweep, and held there, two black arms raised over the glass, and the rain on the windscreen did not run. The meeting in the earphone went quiet, not silent but hushed, like a crowd in a theatre when the lights go down. The streetlamp outside the window, the one that had been passing, was passing still, one slow amber instant stretched across the pane. And in the stillness, in the small warm cave of the cab with its smell of incense and wet vinyl, he heard, distinctly, from somewhere that was not the driver's radio or the street or any machine, a single clear note, like a finger touching the rim of a glass.

Suspended, said the voice at the back of his skull, and it was not clerical now at all. It was a very old, very patient voice, almost fond. One minute. A single minute. I will take it. And then, quietly, to no one: I'm sorry. It was too bright.

He got home at ten past nine, soaked to the knee, with her umbrella under his arm because she had forgotten it and he had pretended not to notice. The flat was dark. The lamp over the desk made its small gold room, and in the gold, the journal lay open where he had left it that morning, with its three pink lines. He sat down without taking off his shoes. His hands were still shaking, and his mouth was still the wrong shape, and somewhere behind his sternum there was a bright, intolerable pressure, as if he had swallowed a lit match and could not decide whether to be afraid.

He began to write. He wrote the corridor, and the hug, and the clip in his hair, and the taxi, the rain on the glass, the laptop on his knees. He wrote Don't increase your walking speed. He wrote the earphone with its tangle of wire. He wrote the way her hands had held his arm, and the sound she made, and the second kiss on her cheek, slower than the first. His hand moved quickly, fluently, as though the words were being poured through him, and when he reached the clock, he wrote the time without thinking: 7:02.
And then he stopped.

The next line was blank. Not empty, not unwritten, but blank, as though a strip of white had been laid across the page by a ruler. It was one line high, a narrow clean band of nothing between 7:02 and the lines that followed, which were in his own hand, in his own black ink, and which began: She said thank you. I said I'd never forget. He had no memory of writing them. He sat with the pen in his fingers and looked at the band of white, and he knew, with the cold certainty of a man reading a verdict, that something had happened in it. Something enormous. That he had been there, and had felt it with his whole body, and that it was gone from the page as completely as a word from a sentence that had been edited by someone who did not know it was important.

He did not remember. That was the strange part. He remembered the cheek and the clock. He remembered the hush of the wipers. He remembered the note like a finger on a glass. But the minute itself, the sixty seconds after 7:02, was a clean white room in his head with the door closed, and he stood outside it with his hand on the handle, and it would not turn.
His phone buzzed on the desk.
It was a notification from Instagram, a small grey banner, and it said, in the flat voice of an app: saumya.shah changed her nickname for you to "duffer <3". The time stamp beneath it read 7:04 PM.

He stared at it. He looked at the clock on the wall, which read 21:14. He looked at the phone, which read 21:14 also, and the notification, which read 7:04, and which had arrived now, two hours late, or two hours early, or from a place where those words had no meaning. He tapped it. The message opened. There was a heart, tiny and pink, and a name he did not recognise as his own, and a short flurry of laughing emoji. And beneath it, from her, a single line, sent at 21:15, one minute in the future, which he read with his eyes and his chest and the whole of his trembling skin:
Don't read too much into it.

He put the phone face down on the desk. He sat there for a very long time. The crane, on its corner of the manuscript, had turned its whole body to face him, and its left wing, the one with the groove, was pressed so deeply into the paper that the crease had split, a tiny white fault like a hair, and through it a thread of light seemed to come from nowhere.

Nothing has been taken, he told himself. Nothing has been taken. I have the clock. I have the cheek. I have the sound of her breath, and the earrings, and the way she said thank you with her eyes closed.

He did not say it aloud. He did not need to. On the page, below the band of white, in the leaning pink hand that was not his, a fourth line had appeared. It was very short. It had been written with a care so gentle that it nearly broke him.
Kept.

chapters.title: The First Sip
paragraphs: Zero woke with a minute missing, the way one wakes with a tooth gone, tongue going again and again to the place where it had been. The journal lay open on the desk beside the crane. The band of white was still there between 7:02 and She said thank you, one line high and perfectly clean, and beneath it in pink the single word Kept. had not moved or faded, only dried, as if someone had meant it. He did not ask the page what had happened inside the white. He had decided in the small hours, somewhere between the lamp and the ceiling, that a man who keeps asking a locked room what is inside it will end by living in the corridor. At the top of the page, where he had written the date the night before, the heading now read Thursday, 2 July 20262, with a fifth digit he had not written, a small extra year hung on the end like a coat on a hook. He looked at it for a long moment, found that he did not mind, and went to find his shoes.

She had texted at 7:40, a single line that arrived with the full weight of her indifference: running late, didn't sleep, don't make a thing of it. He read it standing in the hallway with one shoe on, and understood that she had been awake as long as he had, and that the thing she had asked him not to make a thing of was the thing he was already building a cathedral around. The commute was a catastrophe. Kurla had flooded overnight into a long brown lake, and he waded across it with his trousers rolled to the knee, past a rickshaw drowning with great dignity and a boy selling plastic sheets from a handcart that had become a boat. He reached the office at nine and did what he had not planned to do and had been planning, in some back room of himself, since the platform at Santa Cruz: he signed himself in, and then, without a second thought, he signed her in too, her name before his in the order of the screen, because the thought of her arriving to a red mark on the attendance board made something behind his sternum clench like a fist. It was a small act, a few keystrokes, the sort of thing a person does for a person without ceremony. At 9:37 he called her, standing in the stairwell with the phone against his ear and the rain still ticking in the pipes, and after nine rings a voice answered that was made entirely of sleep, a warm furred syllable that said hmm… hmm…, the sound of a kitten being patted in its basket, and he stood there with his forehead against the cool wall and could not say a word, because he had called to wake her and found he could not, and so he only listened to her breathe for forty seconds, and then said go back to sleep, I've got your login, and she said mm, and the line went quiet in the gentlest possible way.

She arrived at a quarter past eleven, and the first thing he registered was that she was wearing the pink. It was the same pink top, the colour of the inside of a shell, and the same black formal trousers, and he knew them at once with the particular dislocation of seeing a memory walk into a room: this was the outfit from the sixteenth of June, the first day, the one in the photograph he had not taken and had. It was the first thing she had worn since the night he had said it aloud, the first morning after the sentence existed in the world, and he thought she had chosen it on purpose and would never admit it, which was exactly the kind of thing she did. At her wrist hung a bracelet of small pearls, and on her fingers a layered ring that caught the light in tiers, and on the other arm the pink watch, small and bright, its face studded with zircons that threw tiny chips of colour onto her sleeve. She crossed the floor with her laptop against her hip and her eyes carefully on nothing, and sat, and said, "You logged me in," and when he said, "I did," she said, "Before yourself," and he said, "I may have," and she let that sit for exactly as long as it took to open a file, and said, to the screen, "That's a stupid thing to do," in a voice that meant the opposite. Then she reached into her bag, a small zipped pouch he had watched her turn inside out the morning before, the one she had shaken for the earbuds like a woman shaking a sleeping animal, and her hand stopped inside it. "Zero," she said, quite slowly. She drew out her hand, and in her palm lay a small white case, scuffed at one corner, the lid a little yellowed from a hundred nights, and inside it, snug in their cradles, the earbuds. She had searched that pouch twice. He had watched her. She turned the case over, and the left bud rolled a little in its socket, the one that had never worked well, and she looked at him with an expression in which relief and a deeper unease sat side by side like two people who have not been introduced. "They were not here," she said. "I took everything out. I held the bag upside down." He said, carefully, that things were sometimes in the last place you looked. She said, "Not this one." And she put the case against her chest, with both hands, the way she had held the phone and the clip in the cab, and sat for a moment with her eyes closed, and he understood that she was listening for a song.

He did not remember deciding to take her to the staircase, or her deciding to come. At half past one the floor emptied for lunch in its slow, tidal way, and she stood and looked at him over her screen with a small unreadable motion of the head, and he followed her through the fire door and down, past the seventh floor landing, to the place where the concrete stairs turned and the strip lights hummed and the whole world above and below went out of earshot, a narrow well of grey that seemed, by some architectural accident, to have been designed for exactly two people and no more. He put his arms around her. That was all. There was no plan and no preamble, only the simple fact of his arms going round her and her face turning into his collar, and the long shuddering exhale that left both of them at once, as though they had been holding the same breath since the taxi, and in the humming dark of the stairwell time seemed to forget how to move. She kissed his cheek, the smallest peck, a thing so slight and so lightly done that he had no idea how it could feel so heavenly, and something rose in him, an instinct older than speech, and he lifted her. He picked her up, off the concrete, the way a knight lifts a princess from the floor of a flooded hall, because the world beneath her did not deserve the gentle patter of those fair feet, and she gave a startled breathless laugh against his neck and held on. He felt, in that single moment, stronger than he had ever felt in his life, as though he had been made to conquer the world and himself, and not for his own sake but for the weight in his arms. It was not that he was carrying her. It was that he was holding his whole world, and nothing on earth could have persuaded him to put it down. They stayed like that, he did not know how long, kissing forehead and temple and the corner of an eyebrow, careful never to leave the faintest mark, because love should never become a reason for her to answer questions at home. Their feet found each other on the cold stone, his bare and frozen from the flood, hers resting against them without comment, a small symbol of something he had no word for, and somewhere above them a door banged and footsteps began to come down, and they sprang apart like two guilty children and stood against opposite walls with their faces on fire, and a colleague rounded the landing, and looked at them, and looked at the ceiling, and said "Lovely weather," and continued down with the immaculate tact of a person who has seen everything and intends to describe none of it, and when the footsteps had died away they slid down their opposite walls and laughed until they could not breathe, because the building had belonged to them and it had turned out, after all, to belong to a man from Accounts.

First, said the clerical voice, from the long hum of the strip lights, in the tone of a clerk who has begun a new column and is not yet certain what to call it. The subject has yielded priority. Logged her in before himself. Lifted her before steadying himself. There was a rustle like paper. Third instance. Pattern probable. It was not unkind. It was barely anything. It was the sound of a hand drawing a small pink tally mark in the margin of a ledger that had no pages, and Zero, who was still laughing against the cold wall, did not hear it, and would not know for some time what it was counting.

The Ocean drink came after lunch. He had gone down to the corner shop in his lunch hour, in a mood that had no name, and come back with a small paper bag of presents for the floor and for her: Bournville in the dark cranberry-and-raisin wrapper, KitKat Minis in their shining red, a strip of Cofsils in ginger, lemon and orange for a cough that she pretended she did not have. He gave out the sweets like a man throwing flowers at a parade, and the floor lit up, and the office felt warmer, and then he took the last thing out of the bag, a tall cold bottle of Ocean, that bright improbable blue that has never occurred in nature, and he cracked the cap and, before it touched his lips, held it out to her. He did it without thinking. His hand made the decision, the way it had made the decision about the plate on the thirtieth of June, and she looked at the bottle, and at him, and a very small thing happened in her face, a recognition so fast that he almost missed it, and she took it and drank, one long swallow, her throat moving, and gave it back to him with the cold beading on her fingers. You probably didn't even notice, he thought, but I did, and I hope it always stays that way: whatever life gives me first, I want you to have the first taste. It is an honour to share. He put his mouth where hers had been. It tasted of nothing. He frowned at the label, at the cheap blue plastic, and drank again, and again it tasted of nothing, of cold, of water that remembered an idea of citrus, and he thought it was the flood, or the cold he was coming down with, or the slow chemistry of a very long week, and he let it go. I learned that some objects are not objects at all; they are pieces of time that survived. He would write that line one day, in a pink that would not be his, and he would be thinking of this bottle, which she had held and he had held, and of a white case with its bad left bud, and of a black hair clip and a pair of golden hoops and a brooch in a zipped pouch, a whole small museum of the saved, each thing a minute that the world had tried to take back and had somehow failed to. He did not know yet that he had just paid for it. He did not know that every first he gave her was a first he would not taste, that the ledger was keeping its books honestly and that somewhere a small blue taste had been struck from his tongue to be entered under hers. He only knew that she was smiling at him over the neck of an ocean-coloured bottle, and that for the first time he had made a gift of something so small it could not possibly be taken from him.
"You still didn't feed me the KitKat," he said, an hour later, from the desk across from hers, in a voice of formal injury.
"I'm sorry?"

"I offered you the first sip of a drink. I brought you an entire box of chocolates. You have not once, not once, fed me a KitKat with your own hand." He put a hand on his chest. "I am internally protesting. Ouch, bro. Feed me."
"No."
"I'll never forget this."

"I know." She broke a finger of the wafer, looked at it, ate it herself with great ceremony, and slid the remaining three across the desk to his side like a woman paying a ransom in the smallest possible coin. "And you'll never let me forget it either."
"I will not."
"I'm aware." The corners of her mouth were doing something terrible. "That's the entire problem."

He took the three fingers, and when he thought no one was looking he leaned across the divider and pressed his mouth to her temple, behind the screen of two monitors and a pot plant, and she tasted of cherries and strawberries and the waxy sweetness of a lipstick she had applied at the lift. She kissed him back. And again. And somehow every one of them still felt like the first. Under the desk her foot found his, and rested there, and it was warm.

He went to the director's room at three. It was a meeting about the dashboard, one of those long affable rituals in which men in good shirts agree with one another at length, and he sat through it with half his mind on the screen and the other half on the floor outside, on a girl who was working steadily through a data-cleaning script he had given her, and at the end the director turned and said, "And the intern's work on the parser?" and Zero, who had not been invited to speak, found that he had already spoken. He said that the parser had been rebuilt from scratch in three days; that she had caught an error in the regulator's own template; that the OCR engine ran because she had refused to accept the first answer; that if the director wanted a name to put in the report he should put hers at the top, and he should spell it correctly. The director blinked. He said, "That good?" and Zero said, "Better," and heard his own voice with a faint astonishment, because it was the voice of a man standing in front of a bulldozer, and he had not known he had it in him. She did not need anyone to speak for her. She was perfectly capable of speaking for herself, and had, on several occasions, spoken for him. But he loved to celebrate her. He loved the way pride expanded in his chest, like a lung.

At four she found him at the pantry. She did not say hello. She said, in the flat, tactful voice she used for things that needed to be said without being made to feel like a decision, "You mentioned a girl from your old life. The one who keeps writing."

"I did," he said. His mouth went dry. "I was going to tell you. I've been meaning to say that she—" And he took out his phone and held it toward her, screen up, the whole open ledger of it, the messages and the names and every unguarded thing a man keeps in his pocket. It was an offering and a surrender. I will always listen to the love of my life, he thought, and I will always share everything, and I want every wall between us to be made of glass.
She looked at the phone. She did not take it. She put two fingers against its edge and pushed it gently back toward his chest. "I don't need to read it," she said. "I need you to decide."
"Decide what?"
She was silent for a moment. Then she said, with a tact so careful that he could see the effort of it, a woman going out of her way not to make a thing sound like an order, "Block her."

He did not hesitate. That was the part he would remember afterwards. There was a heartbeat in which he might have said wait or let me think or she's only a friend, and there was none; his thumb was already on the screen, and the thing was done, a little grey line, this contact is blocked, and the phone lay quiet in his palm, a lighter object than it had been a minute before. "Done," he said.
She looked at him for a long time. "You didn't have to do it that fast."
"I know."
"No, I mean—" She touched the pink watch at her wrist, a small unconscious gesture, as though to check the time that had just changed. "I didn't want it to feel forced."
"It didn't." And it was true. No one stands above you in my life, he thought. Not my ego, not another person, not even myself. "It felt like the first easy thing I'd done all week."

Priority, said the voice, very quietly, from somewhere behind the coffee machine. Fourth instance. The subject has now yielded a person. And then, in the slow, bruised tone of an accountant who has begun to suspect that the figures are not the problem: He does not seem to feel it as a loss.

They were caught at five, which was inevitable, and which, in retrospect, both of them would insist had been entirely the other's fault. A delivery arrived, a bag of cough lozenges and a bottle of cold water from the quick-commerce app, and the boy who brought it came through the fire door at the wrong moment and found them on the landing of the staircase below the seventh floor in an embrace so thoroughly Titanic that it was only the absence of an ocean that made it ridiculous. He stood there with the bag. He looked at them, and at the ceiling, and at the bag. "Zepto," he said, in a small voice. And she began to laugh into Zero's collar, helplessly, a high silent hiccuping laugh that shook them both, and Zero said "thank you, put it down anywhere," and the boy put it down on the stair as if it might go off, and fled. They did not speak for a full minute. Then she said, into his shirt, "I'm going to be sick," and he said, "Same," and they stood in the humming grey well with their foreheads together and their whole selves shaking, and it was the happiest he could remember being.

The rest of the evening went by in a slow blur of very ordinary work. They muted the Talker for an hour on the shared channel and told themselves it was an accident. They shared the cough lozenges and made faces at the ginger. She kept one eye on him and one on the room, silently making sure nothing in their small secret could be read by a stranger, and he understood all over again that she was fluent in a language of eyebrows and glances that he would spend a lifetime learning. And at six the phone on her desk lit up, and she looked at it, and her face changed. "My parents," she said. "They want me home for dinner. There's a thing. They've decided." She said it with a flat acceptance that did not quite cover something else. "I'm sorry."

He had been looking forward to dropping her home. He had been looking forward to it all day, the walk, the umbrella, one last forehead kiss in the shadow of a mango tree. And for a moment disappointment went through him like a draught from an open window. Then he thought, quite clearly, home is where she is loved too, and the draught closed. "Then we'll book you a cab," he said, and did. They waited in the reception on the cold leather bench, and he took out his phone and held it up, and she leaned in without being asked and the screen caught the two of them, her cheek against his shoulder, her eyes bright, her hair coming loose at one side. Every photograph somehow captures the gentleness she carries without even trying. When he looked at the picture afterwards he thought, with a catch in his throat, that it was a second one, and that the first, the one on the morning of the sixteenth, the pink top and the black trousers and the laugh just off the edge of the frame, he had taken after all. He remembered it now. He had been standing in the doorway with his thumb on the shutter when she turned to leave, and the light had done its trick, and he had pressed the button without thinking and then forgotten, because forgetting was what the thing did. He had taken it. He had always taken it. The Correction had only lent him the surprise.

The cab came. At the kerb he did a thing he had been saving all day. He leaned toward the auto-rickshaw parked beside it, whose driver was idly watching the rain, and said in a ringing public voice, "Excuse me, brother, could I get her live location?" And she turned, scandalised, and cried, "You want my location as well?" and the driver's head came round with a look of such pure and comic horror that Zero had to put his hand over his mouth. "Mission accomplished," he said. She was laughing. She was still laughing as she stepped to the door of the cab, and then she stopped, and turned, and put out her hand, formally, the way two people shake who have decided to become something else. He took it. The handshake lasted a second. And then, with the whole street watching, he leaned forward and kissed her, a single sincere kiss, brief and unhurried, on the cheek, and she gave it back to him on his own cheek, and the little gestures made him fall for her again, a countless number of times, all in one evening.

She got into the cab. She looked out through the rain-streaked glass. One last lingering look, one last silent promise, and then it pulled away into the evening with its yellow light smeared across the wet road, and he stood and watched it go and did not move until it had turned the corner, hoping for only one thing: that she would have a wonderful dinner with her family. My happiness no longer begins with whether I get more time with her, he thought. It begins with knowing she is smiling, safe, cared for, surrounded by people who love her. And if I am fortunate enough to be even a small part of that, then today was a beautiful day.

At home he wrote the entry in the pale light of the lamp, and the pen was steady for the first time in days. He began with the staircase and ended with the cab. I love you with all my heart, Saumya, he wrote at the bottom, her real name, the only time he used it, and he looked at the word on the page with a faint reverence, like a man who has written the name of a country he intends to live in. And this is the entry of the second of July, which made me fall for you another countless number of times. He read it through. The extra digit sat at the top of the page like a small clock that had started to run a little fast, and beneath it, in a hand that leaned like a bird toward a conversation, the pink had added a column of marks, a neat vertical row of tallies, five of them, each one small and careful and as soft as a sigh.

On the desk, the empty Ocean bottle stood beside the crane. He had not thrown it away. He did not remember deciding not to. It was a cheap thing, a blue plastic bottle with a peeling label, and it caught the lamplight in its little curved shoulders and held it, and he picked it up and turned it in his hand, and thought of her throat moving, one long swallow, the cold beading on her fingers. He lifted it to his mouth. There was a last mouthful in the bottom. He drank it, and it tasted of nothing at all, of water and cold and the faint plastic memory of a flavour, and a feeling went through him that was not alarm, only a faint puzzled loneliness, the sense of a man reaching for a stair in the dark and finding it one step lower than he had thought.

Whatever life gives me first, he thought, I want you to have the first taste. He had said it, in the ink, that afternoon. He had meant it as a vow. He had not understood that someone, somewhere, was listening, and taking it as a contract.

He put the bottle down. The crane had turned during the evening, a few degrees, until its beak was no longer pointed at the title or at the window but at the bottle itself, and beneath the pink tallies, in the hand that was not his, a last line had appeared, in a tone so tender that he almost did not see what it cost.
Hers first.
